quotes.verbatim_quote:
To know which voicing to pick we need to establish:

1. The string the melody note is on
2. The type of chord that is in the chord progression whilst that melody note is played
3. The interval of the melody note in relation to that chord.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Gives the three-step lookup procedure that operationalizes the voicing-selection rule into a repeatable workflow.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
“If it’s easy on the hands, the music will flow better - so most of the time making things as easy
as possible is musically the best option anyway”.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Frames ease of execution not as a compromise but as the musically superior choice, justifying simplification decisions throughout the arranging process.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The jazzy sound in arrangements usually comes from adding extensions and tensions to voicings -
particularly to dominant chords.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Identifies the specific harmonic lever — dominant-chord tension — that transforms a 'vanilla' arrangement into a convincingly jazz-flavoured one.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
A good solo guitar arranger simply suggests these elements throughout the performance. Play a
measure of walking bass, followed by a chord line, followed by unaccompanied single lines —
alternating through these different devices gives the ‘illusion’ to the audience of a complete band.

The listener’s mind will fill in the gaps.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the governing aesthetic principle of solo jazz guitar arranging: implication rather than completeness, which shapes every subsequent technique in the module.

quotes.topic: Fingerstyle vs pick for solo guitar
quotes.verbatim_quote:
many of the voicings you are about to learn are quite difficult to play with a pick if
you intend to sound the notes simultaneously without tricky muting techniques. For this reason, I
gravitate to using fingerstyle picking for solo guitar.

But, you can still use these voicings with a pick. Some players strike the bass note first with their pick
then follow up with a strum of the upper notes in the voicing
quotes.why_load_bearing: Addresses the fundamental technique choice for solo guitar and provides a practical workaround for plectrum players.

quotes.topic: Bass notes role in solo guitar
quotes.verbatim_quote:
The key difference between a ‘trio’ chord melody arrangement (to be played in a band) and solo
guitar is the greater prominence of bass notes on the 5th and 6th strings.

You no longer have a bass player to play with, so you need to fill that role ourselves — otherwise, the
arrangement will sound thin and empty.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Identifies the single most important structural difference between trio and solo arranging, making bass-note placement the primary new skill to develop.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
An excellent way around this is to choose a key for your arrangement that allows the use of open
strings - especially for the bass notes.

Choosing a key like A, E, or D gives you essentially another set of free fingers. Without needing to fret
the occasional bass note, you can make things much easier technically.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Gives a concrete, actionable strategy — key choice — for solving the technical difficulty of simultaneous bass and chord voicings in solo guitar.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
These are called shell voicings — i.e. the ‘bare bones’ of what you need to define the sound of the
chord: the root, 3rd, and 7th.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the term 'shell voicing' and its three essential components, which become the foundational building block for all solo guitar arrangements in this module.

quotes.verbatim_quote: You can remove the 5th from the chord and still retain the essential character of the sound.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the harmonic principle that justifies shell voicings — the fifth is expendable — allowing players to reduce fingering complexity without sacrificing chord identity.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Arpeggiation is when you pluck the notes of a chord one at a time, instead of a block of notes
played simultaneously.

This can give a more lyrical sound and is especially effective in arrangements of jazz ballads.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines arpeggiation and specifies its primary musical context (ballads), giving the arranger a clear criterion for when to deploy the technique.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Octaves are a case of doubling the melody one octave down.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Concise definition of the octave technique as used in chord melody, establishing it as a specific melodic-doubling device rather than a chordal one.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
When playing the octaves, mute the unwanted open string between the octave notes by gently
touching the string with your first finger.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Provides the essential left-hand muting technique required to cleanly execute octaves on guitar, without which the in-between string will ring sympathetically.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Diads are when you harmonize a line in a parallel interval, usually 3rds or 6ths.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines diads as a specific parallel-interval harmonization technique and identifies the two most common intervals used, directly setting up the notated examples.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Refining an arrangement is the most important step of solo guitar arranging.

Making small tweaks, cutting unessential notes, and looking for skillful ways to finger passages to get
the arrangement to feel good under the hands and sound good is the aim.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes refinement — not initial harmonization — as the most critical stage of solo arranging, reframing the overall workflow hierarchy.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Choose chord voicings that have the same interval of the melody note as the highest note in the
chord shape.

OR

a voicing that can be slightly adapted to have the melody note as the highest note and still sound
good.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the central rule of the chord-dictionary method — the single criterion that drives every voicing decision in the arrangement process.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
generally you don’t need to place
chords on every melody note for a chord melody.

In fact, less is more — placing chords at key places ‘here and there’ is easier on the hands and is
usually more than enough to imply the harmony beneath the melody line.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes the core density guideline — sparse harmonization is both more playable and more musically effective than wall-to-wall chords.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Cut out notes from the chord - e.g. we could cut that low B to make it easier to change to the
next chord
quotes.why_load_bearing: First in a ranked toolkit for resolving unplayable voicings — drop notes rather than abandon the chord.
